# Demand prediction {#sec-demand-prediction}
To answer the question whether demand can be predicted from calendar, weather and location information alone and if a deep learning approach is justified if increasing the complexity. To predict the demand in a spatial unit at a specific time two models, Neural Network and Support Vector Machines, are trained and compared based on different spatial and temporal units.
To have a baseline of what is expected we use a simple historical average: the mean trip count per spatial unit, time-of-day window and weekday/weekend flag, computed on the training set and applied to the test set. It is evaluated at the resolution of the selected model (community areas at 4h), where its normalized MAE (nMAE) of 0.31 shows that on average the prediction is off by 31% of the actual demand. The two models are assessed and compared using the nMAE and R² on the test set. The nMAE is the mean absolute error divided by the mean demand, which allows for a fair comparison across different spatial and temporal resolutions. R² is the coefficient of determination, which measures how well the model explains the variance in the data. The higher the R², the better the model fits the data. The results of the two models are presented in the following sections.

## Support Vector Machines (SVM)
As we predict a continuous demand value, we use Support Vector Regression (SVR). SVR comes with three different kernel functions which were all tested: linear, polynomial and radial basis function (RBF). The SVR is trained on a subset of the data, as it scales roughly quadratically with the number of samples. In the optimization steps 20,000 rows of the training set are used. The final model is trained on a 50,000-row subsample of the training set and evaluated on the test set.
Four design dimensions are varied, giving 2 × 3 × 2 × 2 = 24 configurations: (i) the spatial resolution (448 census tracts or 77 community areas), (ii) the temporal resolution (1h, 4h or 1d), (iii) the target transformation (none or log1p), and (iv) target encoding ^[Target encoding adds one column containing the mean trip count per spatial unit, computed on the training set, so the model learns whether a location is generally busy or quiet.] (with or without). All 24 configurations are trained and optimized. The full feature set can be found in @tbl-svr-features in Appendix -@sec-app-svr-features. A hyperparameter grid search ensures that for each configuration the best kernel type and hyperparameters are selected.

@tbl-svr-full-grid reports all 24 configurations, sorted by test R². Each row shows only the best of the three kernel families for that configuration: linear, polynomial and RBF are tuned separately, and the one with the lowest validation RMSE is refit and scored on the test set. The comparison is therefore between configurations, not between kernels. @fig-svr-kernel-comparison compares the three families directly. 

The ranking is dominated by community areas, which take the top four places, and by the daily resolution, which holds the two best positions. Sorting by nMAE instead puts daily community-area configurations in all four leading rows. Both effects are intuitive, as for both ttemporal and spatial resolutions, these are the biggest buckets, filtering out small noise.

The best configuration overall is community areas at daily resolution with target encoding^[Dummy encoding was rejected because it would add up to 448 sparse columns, which is computationally expensive given the quadratic scaling of kernel SVR.] on the untransformed target (R² 0.93, nMAE 0.23).  However, a daily total per neighborhood is too coarse for fleet coordination, so we select the next best configuration at a smaller temporal resolution instead: community areas with target encoding, log1p and an RBF kernel, at R² 0.91 and nMAE 0.29. It is the best 4h configuration on both metrics and gives up little against the daily winner. Against the fleet-operator baseline at the same resolution (nMAE 0.31, R² 0.90) it reduces the relative error by 5.7%. 

Three shortfalls remain. The SVR sees only a fraction of the data, and several configurations hit the 50,000-iteration solver cap^[The solver has a maximum number of iterations it can perform before stopping to limit the computation time.] rather than converging, making the reported scores a lower bound. The log1p transform compresses high values and so under-predicts extreme peaks, the baskets that matter most on event days. And at fine spatial resolution the model relies entirely on manual feature engineering which can be seen in the collapse of census tract R² from 0.63 to 0.21 without target encoding. @fig-svr-error-boxplot shows the error distribution per community area.
